Rohu (Labeo rohita) is one of the most commercially important freshwater fish species in the Indian subcontinent, and its life-history traits have been extensively studied in both riverine and culture environments. Under typical rearing conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the eggs of this species hatch into prolarvae after approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days], yielding yolk-sac larvae that measure just a few millimetres in total length. During this early phase, the lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth opens and active feeding on planktonic organisms commences. The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the newly hatched yolk-sac larva following chorion rupture, is remarkably small at 0.0005236 grams [Wwb = 0.0005236 grams], a direct consequence of the modest egg diameter that typically measures around 1 millimetre in related cyprinid species. This minuscule initial mass places the larval rohu among the smallest of the major Indian carps at the moment of eclosion, although subsequent growth is exceptionally rapid.

Field surveys and captive growth trials have provided robust estimates of the species' maximum attainable dimensions. The ultimate total length of Labeo rohita, representing the largest individuals ever documented in natural populations, reaches 200 centimetres [Li = 200 centimetres], a size that rivals the largest members of the genus. Such exceptional specimens are typically found in the deep pools of large rivers such as the Ganges and Brahmaputra, where favourable foraging conditions and reduced fishing pressure allow individuals to approach their asymptotic size. Corresponding to this impressive length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown rohu has been recorded at 45,000 grams [Wwi = 45,000 grams], reflecting the robust, deep-bodied morphology characteristic of this cyprinid. This maximum body mass is achieved only after many years of sustained somatic growth, with the most massive individuals often exceeding a decade in age. These values underscore the considerable growth potential of rohu relative to other Indian major carps like Catla catla and Cirrhinus mrigala.

The onset of reproductive capability in female rohu is marked by distinct size thresholds that have been documented across multiple river systems and aquaculture facilities. The total length at puberty for females, the point at which vitellogenesis begins and the ovary becomes capable of producing mature oocytes, is approximately 58 centimetres [Lp = approximately 58 centimetres]. Fish of this size are typically between two and three years of age depending on local thermal and nutritional regimes. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for females, representing the body mass at which gonadal recrudescence is first observed, is estimated at 1,100 grams [Wwp = 1,100 grams]. This value is derived from the allometric relationship between length and mass, as pubertal females exhibit a body condition similar to that of mature adults. Reaching this reproductive threshold is contingent upon adequate food availability and optimal thermal conditions, as slow-growing individuals may delay maturation considerably. The attainment of sexual maturity thus represents a critical life-history transition for this species.

Reproductive output in Labeo rohita is closely tied to the warm monsoon season, when environmental conditions trigger spawning activity. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a single gravid female can release approximately 8,219 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 8,219 eggs per day], reflecting the species' high fecundity relative to its body size. This daily fecundity translates into a spawning season that may last several weeks, with females producing multiple batches of eggs over the course of a single reproductive period. Alongside fecundity, the frequency of spawning events is also critical to understanding total reproductive output; field observations indicate that females typically spawn once per year [F_R_i = once per year], during the peak of the southwest monsoon when river levels rise and dissolved oxygen concentrations are favourable. This annual rhythm synchronizes egg release with optimal conditions for larval survival, as the resulting yolk-sac larvae and free-swimming fry encounter abundant planktonic food resources. The combined effect of high daily egg production and a constrained annual spawning window defines the species' reproductive strategy.

Longevity records for wild populations of Labeo rohita indicate that individuals can attain considerable ages under favourable conditions. The maximum lifespan for this species has been estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years], a figure consistent with growth-ring analyses from scale and otolith samples across its native range at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This lifespan, observed under the thermal conditions typical of tropical river systems, represents the total duration from zygote formation to natural senescence. During this extended period, rohu undergo a complete ontogenetic trajectory from the yolk-dependent prolarva through the exogenously feeding pelagic larva, the fingerling stage, and finally the sexually mature adult. The longevity record of 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days] places rohu among the longer-lived Indian major carps, with individuals often continuing to grow slowly even after reaching reproductive maturity at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Such longevity, combined with high fecundity and a relatively early age at first reproduction, contributes to the species' considerable population resilience in its natural habitat.
